The story’s metaphors connect class mobility with labor and control: Miss Emily treats Nora as “an underperforming subsidiary acquired in a hostile takeover,” while Nora recognizes her new domestic role as “a shift management of the soul.” These comparisons reveal that her apparent escape from service work may instead be its transformation. The allusion to “a refugee from a Chekhov play” also sharpens Miss Emily’s cultured, cutting voice while underscoring Julian’s ineffectual intellectualism.
